demo: {Ruler} governs {place}. Its word is given by {whoEnd}.
{Ruler} governs {place}. Anyone with business before it goes to {whoEnd}.
{Ruler} governs {place}. {whoEnd} answers for how it is run.
Ask who governs {place} and the answer is {ruler}. Ask who decides, and the answer is {whoEnd}.
Rows of brick dry under cover until there is enough to fire. Work stops when the clay runs out.
A firing eats more fuel than any hearth in the village, and takes a day and a night to cool.
Its brick goes into chimneys, floors and walls meant to outlast the people who raise them.
Hot, dirty work at the pit and the kiln, done by one family and whoever they can hire for a firing.
The criminal houses here have no friend at the head of {power}, and they know it.
Money from a criminal house buys nothing at the top of {power}.
A criminal house that wants something from {power} has to win it in the open, like anyone else.
Take it as settled: whoever runs {power} answers to no one in the underworld.
Officers in the same coat on every main street, about one for every hundred people.
The watch works in shifts, so the streets are walked by night as well as by day.
Its pay comes out of the city's dues, and every year someone says it costs too much.
Most officers know the streets they walk, and the people who live on them.
The street smells of drying herbs and vinegar from one end to the other.
Buyers walk the length of the street before they choose, and the shops know it.
Most of the trade is ordinary: poultices, fever draughts, a salve for a burn.
The shop that sells imported medicines keeps them behind the counter and names its price only when asked.
Few customers, and most leave without buying: the smallest charm costs a craftsman a month's pay.
The scribe works at a slanted desk by the best window, and one slip spoils the whole sheet.
A greater working is written to order, paid half in advance; it costs a merchant a year.
A single scroll can take days of careful copying.
Whatever {other} wants from {ruling}, it asks through {face}, who sits in both.
{face} hears the business of {ruling} before it is decided, and {other} hears it soon after.
If {face} gave up either place, {other} would lose most of the weight it carries here.
Members of {other} go to {face} first when they want something from the rulers here.
The door is locked at night, though nobody inside has been charged with anything.
Its yarn and ground meal sell cheaply, and the town's own trades complain of it.
Those who enter give up their own clothes and work in the house's.
Gruel at dawn and at dusk, and a day of grinding or hauling in between.
A long straight walk behind the shop, where the strands are twisted as the ropemaker walks backward.
Well, cart and plough all need its rope, and the hay is tied with its twine.
The finished coils hang from pegs and are sold by the length.
Hard on the hands: a ropemaker's palms are as rough as the hemp.
A horn from the road gives the yard a few minutes to have fresh horses ready.
The fare buys a seat and a meal; a bed is extra, and most passengers do not stay.
Ostlers, a cook and a clerk with the coach book: the house runs to the timetable, not to the guest.
News comes in with every coach, and the waiting room hears it before the rest of the town.
The vats stain the dyer's arms to the elbow, and the ground behind the shop is never one colour.
A deep red or a true blue costs far more than brown, and most of the village wears brown.
Cloth comes in grey from the looms of half the village and goes home in colour.
On a dyeing day the smell of the vats reaches the next house.
